segments: Ghiyath al-Din was astounded {OCR?}:
he took his wife and his children,
and went and fortified himself in the city of Ankara.
Now the Tatars, when they saw that without a blow they had abandoned their pitched tents and fled,
thought that there was treachery involved,
and that they had turned aside as though to lie in ambush.
And when they had waited a day,
and sent scouts and verified that their flight was not a feint,
then they were emboldened and entered the pavilions and plundered everything they found.
And they spread out through the lands of the Romans (Rūm).
And they came first to Sebastia (Sivas),
and the people who were in it submitted to them,
and brought out much gold,
and redeemed their lives from slaughter,
and their sons and their daughters from slavery.
And the Tatars entered the city,
and emptied the royal treasures,
and took away everything that pleased them,
and burned the weapons of war,
and dismantled the walls about forty cubits all around.
Then another division went to Caesarea,
and its inhabitants were not willing to surrender it.
Then all of them gathered against it,
and with mangonels they breached its wall,
and entered it.
And they emptied the royal treasures,
and burned the marvelous palaces,
and tormented the nobles and freemen,
and pierced them with swords,
until they stripped them of all their money.
And afterwards they killed many tens of thousands in it,
and carried away the young boys and girls into captivity.
Now the mother of Sultan Ghiyath al-Din, when she heard of the defeat,
took her daughter, the Sultan's sister,
and her menservants and her maidservants and her treasures,
and entered the country of Cilicia,
and took refuge with the Baron Constantine, the father of King Hethum,
the one who had also been urged by the Sultan to come to his aid,
and he had delayed until he saw the end of the matter.
Now when the Tatars heard that the Sultan's mother was there,
they sent an envoy and demanded her from the bailli, the father of the King.
And some say
that the bailli, wishing to please the Tatars,
sent word to them: 'Behold, so-and-so is with me {OCR?};
send that I may deliver her to you.'
And as soon as the envoys arrived,
they handed her over into the hands of the Tatars.
And this improper deed appeared very hateful and reprehensible in the eyes of all kings and nobles.
And that queen was carried away into captivity,
